When the National

, OPPOSITION TO Insurance Bill was THE INSURANCE introduced into the BILL House of Commons, it received what looked iike an enthusiastic welcome from both parties. We expressed same doubt at thed time as to whether the Conservative acclamations would be continued through later stages. The suspicion may, at any time, have seemed to be ungenerous; but it has since been most amply justified. What was clearly apprehended by the whole House of Commons was that Mr.LLovn GEORGE was paling really great proposals, unprecedented in their character, and designed to bring about a great social uplifting of the people It was impossible to meet such a measure as* the National Insurance Bill with one plain negative. Those who did not like it on the ground that it was produced by their political opponents were really limited to one course. They could applaud the measure as whole in the first instance, and then fight it in detail at the later stages. And this, it be noticed, is what is being done. On Wednesday, Mr. AUSTIN CHAMBERLAIN moves to leave out that portion of the Bill -which deals with the subject of sanatorium treatment of consumption. He was much snore straightforward than is common in such cases. He admitted that he supported the Bill on the sec ond reading without saying -anything about the objection which he now raised. Since then, as he said, he has -changed his mind. Let as take his sincerity for granted, and then ask whether he has good reasons for holding his present views. The sub-section dealing with sanatoria treatment is, Mr. CHAMBERLAIN now thinks, -an excrescence on the Bitl. It will cause the expenditure of a great deal of money, and there is as much reason for treating cancer in the special manner promised as for treating Aconsumption. So Mr. AUSTEN CHAMBERLAIN would take the consumption proposals out of the Bill if he could. Mr. Muxuo FERGUSON, who is not an unwavering friend of the Government, and had no party purpose to cserve, made a crushing reply when he said that, unhappily, we knew too little about cancer, buttwe knew how to fight consump- tion, and the only practical way of doing it is through a general effort such as that con- templated in the Bill. To this, a high medical authority, Dr. ADDISON, contended that there are sufficient data to more than justify THE CHANCELLOR OF THE EXCHEQUER ia setting up sanatoria for the treatment of consumption. The least that can be said, therefore, is that in making his change of mind, Mr. AUSTEN CHAMBERLAIN has not been well advised.

We cannot consent to regard Mr. 'CHAMBERLAIN'S opposition to this portion of the Bill, and Mr. WALTER LONG's support •of the views set forth, as merely individual -expressions of opinions. The general attitude of the Conservative party towards the Bill .of the CHANCELLOR OF THE EXCHEQUER is one of hostility. We turn for proof of this etatement to the election literature which is being issued from the Conservative head- quarters. Mr. LLOYD-GEORGE has found it .necessary to describe a leaflet which is being used in the present bye-elections in very etrong terms indeed. It is a leaflet designed to convince the agricultural labourer that he will suffer under a measure which was bailed on its introduction by loud acclama- tions from the party which is now, in print and otherwise, misrepresenting Mr. LLOYD- GEORGE'S Bill to the electors. It would be Idle to ask if this is honest. Of course it is not. But if it is not honest, what is it?

WARRINGTON elf;f3Sed;inWill; WaeL , BRIDGE: rington Corporation WHY THIS DELAY? 811 l reo6ivett the Rojral Assent, many' towns- , ' people are impatiently asking why there are no signs of a start *frig made with the new bridge works. We are informed that the terms of the contract have been finally settled with the contractors (Messrs. Thorne and Sons, of toandon), and that, as far as they are concerned, operations can commence at any time. All that now stands in the way of progress is the clause inserted in the Act at the instance of the Board of Trade, which provides that " the work shall not commence without the previous consent in writing, under the hand of one of the secretaries or assistant secre- taries, of the Board of Trade." On the day after the Bill received the Royal Assent the Corporation applied to the Board 01 Trade and have since repeatedly pressed them to give their written sanction, but up to the present it has not been forthcoming. How- ever it would appear very unlikely that this necessary formality can be much longer delayed, and there are strong hopes that a start will be made with the new bridge next week.

If many Warrington THE PEaFtor M.P. people present at Bridge Foot on Saturday even- ing held the opinion that Mr. Harold Smith, M.P., was far from perfect, they should be converted by now, because Mr. Harold Smith spent a considerable time in reciting his virtues. In fact over half a column of the valuable space of our contemporary is occupied by the eloquent panegyric on Mr. Harold Smith by himself. It is a most faithful 'bit of reporting, and we do not thinkone single sweet syllable has 'nen missed. Mr. Smith told his audience that he won the election in Warrington because" he fought fair. If he had struck one false note, hit one dirty blow,he would never have been elected." Bravo Harold I " Furthermore he did not think anyone would venture to say that he had said anything that he ought not to have said." 01), paragon We suppose calling Mr. Havelock Wilson a 'paid hack" and a liar was the height of refinement and political courtesy. Now, Mr. Smith is self- pledged to the poor and the working classes. He had never given a vote in the House of Commons without asking himself the question every time " Will it improve ' the lot of the workingclasses." Magnificent! The lords and the lawyers, the landowners and the brewers, and their many separate and united interests, never cross the mind of the altruistic Member for Warrington. "Think always of the people "is his own political root idea, for has he not told us so, and rejoiced openly in the thousands of horny Warrington hands that he has clasped in friendship and brotherliness during the seven months of his representation of the good old town. What more can a man do or say, to secure the votes of the proletariat so long as he remains convinced that soft soap is their staple diet?

As a pedestrian public NEEDLESS NOISES, we have become inured, and more or less resigned, to the diversity and in some cases hideous nature of the noises produced by motorists to give 'audible warning" of their approach. They are largely a necessity for the preservation of life and limb, but there is not the slightest justification for the weird mechanical syren which many cyclists have equippsd themselves with of late. It emits an ear-piercing wail suggestive of a soul in torment and ' causes the hapless pedestrian to jump in an unpleasant and I undignified fashion. Some of these wheelers I—usually rather young—appear to fancy themselves 40 h.p. six cylinder motor-cars, and rouse up the public accordingly. They are becoming so great a nuisance that we are hopeful the police may find some grounds for intervention. People now-a-days have reason to remember with heartfelt sympathy the lines by Oliver Wendell Holmes: " And silence like a poultice came To heal the blows of sound."
Tariff Reformers are TARIFF REFORMERS everlastingly trying to AND BRUNNER excite the wrath of the MONO'S.
British public against

the success of the firm of Brunner Mond. According to them, the scientific discoveries of the late Dr. Ludwig Mond, the scientific and technical resource of their chemists, the commercial enterprise and business skill of the firm, have nothing to do with its success. According to this month's Tariff Reform "Monthly Notes," all their profits are due to the fact that they have "secured the British market to themselves." The Tariff Reform argument of course is that if Messrs Brunner Mond were subjected to foreign competition they would not be able to make the tremendous profits out of the British public that they are able to show from year to year. Of course Tariff Reformers cannot allege that any monopoly is given to them by the process of taxing foreign imports. They say Brunner Mond's have secured the monopoly for themselves by agreement with foreign chemical manufac- turers. Supposing that were the case,that is no reason why the British public should tax itself in order to give other firms in other businesses an equal monopoly. Two or three reflections arise out of the argument of the Tariff Reformers. In the first place, it now clearly appears that the object of their pro- tective tariff is to enable privileged manu- facturers all round to make profits like Brunner Mond's. In the second place these privileged manufacturers, shareholders, and capitalists are going to have done for them out of the public taxes what Brunner Mond's have done for themselves. In the third place, when one firm like Brunner Mond's makes profits on the scale they make them it is an injury to the "market they control." But if, by legisla- tive enactment, you can put it in the power of a large number of firms to bleed the British buyer by exlluding foreign competi- tion it at once becomes a blessing to the British werking man, a means of' cementing the Empire," and means a lower income tax, no workhouses, Dreadnoughts paid for by the foreigner, Monte Carlo for artisans, diamond tiaras for workingmen's wives, a new heaven and a new earth, as well as con- siderable improvements even in "the other place." Finally, it is at any rate interesting to learn from the Tariff Reformers that there is at least one British firm which can hold its own against all the world without asking the Tory Government to come to their rescue and give them the "power to negotiate," which, according to them,Tariff Reform alone provides.

Lord Iveagh, who has made such a splendid gift to the King for Dublin hospitals, has spent an immense fortune in benefactions to the poorer classes of his countrymen, both in England and Ireland. The principal I partner in the famous brewery of Guinness, I which he has built up to its present dimen- sions—earning over a million a year in profits and paying about twice as much in revenue to the 'Treasury—Viscount I veajgh has distri- buted about two million pounds for charitable objects.

Alderman Bennett had the unique dis- tinction on Saturday of presiding for Mr. and Mrs, A. H. Crosfield in the afternoon and for Mr. Harold Smith, M.P., in the evening. He appeared to be equally happy on both occasions. _ _ _

We hear from the Tariff Reformers less about boots end shoes than we used to do. The reason is that according to a reply to a question in the House of Commons the other day the imports of boots and shoes "of leather, or of which the chief value is leather," amounted, in 1903 to £881,000; while in 1910 they were only £631,000. 'During the same period, exports of boots and shoes, the manufacture of the United Kingdom, rose from 4845,000 in 1903 to £3,030,000 in 1910.

It is curious with what persistence Alder- man Sennett sticks to an idea, even if proved fallacious. Presently he will be entirely alone in the belief that (as he said on Satur day) Canada is being "dragged from the orbit of the Empire," and will eventually be annexed by the United States. Canadians have no fear of such a fate, and would be amused at the Warrington Alderman's 'ion- cern were they aware of it. * * _

The Lord Advocate, in a speech at Becken- ham on Saturday, said the constitutional crisis was at an end. The Peers knew and the Tory party knew that it was impossible for His Majesty's Ministers to touch the Parliament Bill as it came amended from the House of Lords. The Government would consent to no material change, and to no modification which would in the smallest degree impair the strength and efficacy of the measure. They had set their hands to the task of putting the House of Lords in its Proper place, and they intended to complete that task.

A sigh of relief Must have come from Unionist members when they learned the figures of the West Ham election. The last thing they desired was victory (writes the London correspondent of the "Liverpool Daily Post and Mercury,") and they have happily escaped the danger. Success in Glasgow or West Ham might have encour- aged the hot heads among the peers to hold out and maintain the fight to the bitter end, but that encouragement has been denied to them, and the electors have shown in a remarkable way that the opinion of the country remains absolutely steady. Edward Prince of Was, the central figure in the ceremony at Carnarvon, is the eighteenth who has borne that title, the most illustrious perhaps of any heir-apparent in the world. Eight of them have been named Edward, while there have been among them three Georgee, three Henrys, two Charleses, one Arthur, and one Frederick. It would probably be generally agreed that the most famous, as Princes of Wales, were the Black Prince and the Princes known afterwards as Henry V., George IV., and Edward VII. The last-named was Prince of Wales longer than any other, more than sixty years, but George IV. ran him close, and the Black Prince was third with forty-six years. ,

Th.n monstre picnic of the Women's Liberal Association on Tuesday was a triumph oforganization and a splendid tante to the solidarity and political enthusiasm of the lady members of the party. Our women Liberals have always borne themselves bravely whether in work or warfare, but the spirit was never better than it is to-day. The little chapter of blunders which culminated in the loss of the seat last December has led to a revival in all ranks, and it will be a much more efficient and determined force which takes the field on behalf of Liberalism at the next election. Mr. and Mrs. Crosfield are both giving an inspiring lead, and if loyalty and labour can win the day it will be won for the progressive party, despite all the bluster and brewing on the other side.

A correspondent draws our attention to the fact that the Warrington tram-tickets issued to children "over 3 and under 14 years" are embellished with a large type advertisement which says "Ask for Walker's Pale Ale." This is either misdirected or very clever advertising—we are not quite sure which. It looks like an insidious attempt to undermine the good, but flexible, resolutions of a class of people who are, almost without exception, lifelong teetotallers. Imagine the parental horror if gentle Jane or dutious David should come home to dinner with a hoarse' demand for pale ale. What good is the home or the school teaching going to be if the youthful mind is assailed by temptation in so brazen a manner and in such thirsty weather? This is a serious case for the city fathers (and all other fathers) and we regret that it cannot be put into the hands of the Rev. A. M. Mitchell with full primitive powers.

• • This is called a " strenuous " age; and at the first glance the comparison of George IV.'s visit to Ireland with that of George V. seems to justify the epithet. The other George took a fortnight in getting to Ireland, nearly a fortnight for the return journey— by coach and yacht—and had about three weeks of festivities in between. There and back took him nearly sever. weeks. George V. does it all in Sae days. The contrast is significant of the way we live now in an age which is called "strenuous," but is really full of labour-saving devices. These five days, compared to those seven weeks, simply I mean that we do more at less expenditure of time, temper, and money than our ancestors could achieve. And those who complain of the hustle of the times should remember that they share with the King those conveniences that have enabled him to do in five days a great deal more than his predecessor did in seven weeks—and with less fatigue. • _ •

Carnarvon Castle, to which so many eyes have been turned this week, was called by an old Welsh antiquary "the most magnificent badge of our subjection," and is the most splendid specimen of medieval military archi- tecture surviving in Britain, not except- ing Alnwick. Art and beauty were combined with strength by De Elfreton, the architect, who had been commanded to construct a palace within an impreg- nable fortress. Whether the mean little passage-chamber in the Eagle Tower was the birthplace of the infant prince whom Edward I. made the medium of such a grim practical joke upon the Welsh seem doubtful; but the main story may still be true. Every famous soldier who helped to make history in this corner of Britain has played some part within or without the walls of Catnarvon Castle. It has been starved into surrender, but never captured by force of arms, and can therefore claim to be considered a " virgin fortress."

THE GREAT WHITE PLAGUE.
HOPE FOR CONSUMPTIVES.
[By C. E. Parker.]

The advance made during recent years in the treat- ment of this disease has proved that it in preventible in its inception, and •rrestable hi its early progress It has been shown that the germs cannot thrive as pure air, hence the open air cure. Allow triture fair chance, anpplement it by prnper Ii gienic measures under medical advice and the mirtaliiy from this scourge could be redtmed to a minimum. What is perhaps more important is that by a more healthy and natural condition of life the inception of the disease might be prevented. Bad housing, improper clothing, insufficient nourishment, inherit- ance, and environm at have in many case. devitalized the power of resistance, especially amongst the poorer classes. The conditions surroutding the life of a con- sideratile propoition of our people are unhealthy, and tend to the development of the disease, this e.tpec.ally 00 111 towns. But many if these c-tndit ions are under our ci,n control, and could be remedied, some by individual, sad aortae by collective action. Take the conditions in the room, in which many sleep, spend- ing in this way about one-third of their rime. There are too often over-crowded, but the had effects of thin are frequently accentuated by doors and window, not only being kept shirt, but by various methods such as door mats, window rolls and the like, to keep out the fresh air and imprison the liad sir. Nature is ever carrying on, by a balance of wonderful lawn a constint movement of the atmosphere which if we do not impede contributes to health and well-bring. But too many iho all in their power to frustrate the beneficent action of there law.. The air should be continually changed to get rid of the impoverialied and impure atmosphere contaminated by the breath, and other exhalations from the body, arid replaced by air con- taining its full proportion of oxygen. Nt.t only is the air rolzbed of its oxygen by the human body, lint !gas lights and lamps act in much the IRMO way,consuming what is most valuable in the air and replacing same by the formation, in the burning, of anhealthv gases. A. a rule the living room of a house is fairly well ventilatt d eapecially where there is a fire which is constantly changing the air. It is the bedroJma in which there is the greatest danger. Their have, as a rule, no fire to change the Mr ; if there is a grate it ia generally blocked, and unless die window, and if practicable the door, is °pea, the impoverished

, air is breathed over an! over again. Every bedroom window ought to be clan, preferably at the top and in all weathers. A good plan is to board up inside the bottom cill, say a couple of inches, which will allow the bottom numb to open and allow air to come in at the middle, and hecsnee of the relative positions of the two sash's the draft is sent upwards and so distributed. With many who live in the smoky . .

parts of Warrington the ditliitilty will at once ',resent itself that in freely admittitg fresh air you also freely Omit fresh diii I hive no new remedy for this. The existing one o insisting that th se yam make srimke should turn it into power or hest instead of turning it into the atmosphere is the only remedy, and pubic opinion should be strong enough to enforce it. It is a well.known fact that there is much less

tuberculosis amongst high cattle than in the cattle of England and Scotland. And it is probably rightly attributed to the fact that Irish cattle spend almost the whole cf their time in the open, being h.i.ed only milt of the wilber, while in England and Scotland they are very much more c,tifii.ed. On the 'tiler livid there is a much hiuher human mortality (nearly double) from coninimption in Ireland than in England and Scotland and this mny be attributed largely to the f..ct that the housing conditions in Ireland ore, or have been much worse than thus, on our side, bad as these are in many quarters. Happily with tl,e improved !rinsing conditions in Ireland•distinct improvement is already unwires,.

Irt regard tt those wh, have contract ci die disease fresh air tree meat is absolutely essential. la the case of many it is unh Ipail7 alto tot impossible to leave home and take advantage of the excellent Sanatoria which are springing up in diffetentrirts of the country. But it should not be supposed that it is impossible to combat the disease by th se who live in an ordioary Louse. In the day time the !patient should be in the open-air every brain that is possible, and almost in al weathers. When obliged to be inside (ors all windows almuld be open back arid front to admit of a through air current, of course regulated by commonsense. The patier,t should be warmly, but not too warmly, clad in wool'. clothing. Ile should not be afraid of work, or exercise, in moderation, work or rxercise that induces deep breathing is good. Dust should be avoided as it tends to irritate the lung..

It is a mistakelo think that it is necessary to kaee this country u ith its damp atmosphere to go to some high altitude, a dry atmosphere, and abundant sun- shine before scare can be affected. These conditions are without doubt helpful and in some cases almost essential. But coneomptives have been cured in the most unlikely climates, and what is of far more

importance tlt'an the climate, is the use that is made of it Many things point to the conclusion that freah air, knowledge of the conditions, and suitable medical Impel Vinlol3 are more impotent than a fine climate. lack of fresh air is the grestent predisposing cause of consumption, fresh air is the most potent mean• of rent°, 'log the patient to health I trust therefore the State aid that is to be given to the budding of !Sanatoria will tilt have the elect or divertiog atten- tion from the possibility of preventing the inception of consuropion, and the curing of it in the early stlyte• in the homes. If intelligent rare were taken by individuals in the localities in which they live theta would be little need to build a single additional aanatorium. When all has been add about fresh air it in well to remember it in far from everything ; poor living, bad cooking, illnutrition, dirt, destitution, are all causes which le-sen the vitality which is the surest safe- guard against thin and all other iliseasies. Everyone who wages war against those evils which impair the vitality of the people is belying, although indirectly, the work of exterminming the great white plague.

div.head: ROYAL VISIT TO IRELAND.
div.p: THE ROYAL VISIT TO IRELAND.

Amid scenes of great enthus;asm the King and Queen, with the Prince of Wales and Princess Mary, made their state entry into Dublin on Saturday. Thousands of people cheered them when they went ashore at Kingstown, where they were received by the Lord Lieutenant and Lady Aberdeen, and numerous off icials. From Kingstown to Dublin Castle, a drive of about 9 miles, the route was densely packed with peoa'e, an I the appe. trance of the Royal party was alw iys a signal for a great outburst of cheering The decorations were very fine, and Dublin never looked more spfendid. Banners and devices wishing their Majesties a long and prosperous reign were to be seen on every side. Their Majesties have spent • busy time. Their engagements included the opening of the Royal College of Science, a Levee at Du'alin Castle, Leopardstown Races, Holding a Chapter of the Order of St. Patrick, and Review of Troops sad Presentation of Colours. Our pictore shows the Royal procession at College Green.
THE INVESTITURE OF THE PRINCE OF WALES,

Carnarvon Castle, the scene of the Investiture of the Prince of Wales, was built by Edward I. in 1281. Within the Castle the spacious courtyards have had built upon them wooden structures affording accommodation for some 8,000 spectators. The Prince will be received at the Eagle Tower by the Right Hon. Lloyd George and other officials; a procession will then be formed of G:ntlemen Ushers, Moyors of 28 Welsh boroughs, and 25 Welsh bLP.'s. After parsing between the Lords bearing the Regan., the Prince will be conducted to the King, who will perform the actual ceremony. Our photograph shows the Castle front the sea. Inset is of the Prince, and on the right may be seen the Queen Eleanor Gateway, where the Prince will show himself to the populace after the Ceremony.

div.head: HENLEY REGATI A.
div.p: HENLEY REGATI A.

The Henley of 1911 will be remembered as one of the most successful and most brilliant regattas in history. It was not only the fine weather and gaol ...ming that made the carnival so enjoyable, it was the fact that English rowing had gat back ta its old high standard of efficiency. A picturesque and unusual s,g'at was the appearance of a war canoe of the Maoris, paddled by women as well as by men. They made a wonderful picture of barbarism in their qnaint native dress. The boat was decorated with all kinds of war ornaments, and loud cheers greeted them as they paddled up the cour C.

PILGRIMAGES

div.head: MAL PAS AND 1 HEREA BOUTS.
div.p: MAL PAS AND 1 HEREA BOUTS.

Our mention last week of the quiet Cheshire town known as Malnas, took concern only for its most famous son. But other memories and stories linger here that well merit re-telling. Before we quit the old Rectory, the birth- place and home of Bishop Heber, we recall the Billion's extraordinary brother.

div.head: BIBLIOPHILE OR BIBLOMANIAC.
div.p: BIBLIOPHILE OR BIBLOMANIAC.

..... Reginald Heber, Rector of Malian, was twice married, and Richard, born in 1773, was the son of his first wife. He inherited property which placed him in a good position and hopes were entertained that he might enter public life, but it soon became evident that his sole thought was centreing in the hobby of book collecting. The only thing that would draw him to London was a book sale, and he began to build up a library of curious old works relating to the English poets and dramatists. When the battle of Waterloo brought peace to Europe, he started upon a tour of Belgium, France and the Netherlands, in each place making large purchases of books. Sale rooms and book- sellers' shops were the only places that had any charm for him, and since it was difficult to send the big consignments of volumes to England, he purchased or rented houses in which to store them. Book hunt- ing filled his life. On hearing of a curious book he would take a mail-coach journey of three or four hundred miles to secure it, fearful to entrust the task to any other. The mania grew apace. He not only bought to secure curious books, but bought to keep them from others. Increasing age ' strengthened the passion for possession, and not content with having the largest private collection of old English books, he built up the largest collection ever made by one indi- vidual of foreign books also. He had four houses in England completely filled from cellar to attic with hooks, and every chair groaning under "piles of erudition." Abroad he had houses in Paris, Antwerp, Brussels, and Ghent all similarly filled. When Heber died in 1833 there was keen curiosity to know what would become of his library. He had been too much wedded to books to ever marry a wife and it was anticipated that he would bequeath his books to the nation.
Long search had to be made among his piles of papers before a will was found, and then to the astonishment of everyone it was discovered that his library was not even mentioned.

His executors decided to sell the books and began with the English store. A catalogue of two thousand large pages was prepared and for two hundred and two days the auctioneer toiled to sell them. Nearly 120,000, volumes were thus disposed of and brought in £57,000. But the Continental libraries were left to (heir fate. It is estimated that Heber had collected in all 500,000 volumes and had spent £250,000 in obtaining them. A few minutes spent upon a document would have secured a valuable gift to the nation and made scholars grateful for ever. The man who had spent forty years upon a single oblect neglected (passing strange!) the one thing that would have given it value.

div.head: GOOD MALPAS STORY,
div.p: A GOOD MALPAS STORY,

" Quaint and charming "are adjectives that flow easily and often from the pen when Cheshire villages are to be described. In the case of Malpas they are most fittingly applied. Its fine embattled church is placed upon the top of a hill and its two streets are lined with old and irregular houses.

One of these is the "Red Lion," and the pilgrim who likes to imbibe history with his liquors may find it plentifully provided and with the addition (if we dare suggest it) of an improving dash of tradition. King James is the hero of the "Red Lion." Very thirsty he called one day and entered the tap roam. Here "supping their beer, at the Rector and curate enjoying good cheer." The king joined them and toasts and merri- ment became the order of the afternoon. It came in turn to the Rector to pay, but he refused to pay for the curate exclaiming " Higgledy piggledy Malpas shot I Let every tub stand on its own bottom."

The King was well versed in Cheshire sayings and cried out, " Nay, nay, Maxfield measure, heap and thrutch." But tile rector I would not yield, so the King paid for the curate himself and went his way. Before long the curate was by royal appointment made joint rector of Malpas and the Rector 'found that his curate had been made his I equal. Such is the legend of the double I Certain it is that Malpaa for generations had two rectors and the anomaly remained until another church was built and the living divided.

div.head: MALPAS CHURCH.
div.p: MALPAS CHURCH.

The church of Maims, strong and massive without,has some interesting things within. It has a fourteenth century pricina, some fine old oak stalls and a great chest decorated with chased ironwork. The two chapels are those of the Cholmondeley family and the Breretons. The first mentioned contains ancient monuments which are splendidly preserved and the second contains the body of Randle Brereton and his wife. It was their son who figured in the shameful tragedy which brought Anne Boleyn to the scaffold. Sir William Brereton was the one against whom the charge of intrigue was made by the fierce and unfeeling Henry VIII, a false charge no doubt, but Henry did not hesitate to sacrifice a faithful servant to gain his ends.

div.head: .HERO OF THE PLAGUE.
div.p: A .HERO OF THE PLAGUE.

The parish register of Malpap contains at least one unusual entry.lt is indhed a story of heroism and one can be grateful to the clerk who took the unusual course of recording it there.ln the tiny village of Bradly near by in the year 1625 there lived a Richard Dawson,a humble man and poor. The plague was 'devastating Cheshire and he found himself 'smitten by it. He was a heavy man; to quote the register "heavier than his said nefew and another wench were able to bury." He realized what his death would mean at a time when panic reigned and what difficulty it would place upon his nephew and maid. Rising from his bed with his remaining strength he dug a grave near his house. Calling to his nephew to place some straw at the bottom, he lay down "and so departed out of this world.'. He was not only a big man but strong, says the clerk. So he was in a far better sense than the scribe intended, and we are glad for the story. .

div.head: COMBEHMERE.
div.p: COMBEHMERE.

We leave Malpas to run 'to Whitchurch and drop down at once to No Man's Heath. From this point onwards the pilgrim may find many places of beauty and interest. Cholmondeley Park gloriously wooded and with half-a-dozen pools and lakes invites us to turn aside. Then there is Marbury with its lovely mere, which covers twenty-one acres in which is reflected the image of its beautiful church. Combermere must by no

means be missed and we pick our way to the site of the Abbey that overlooked its waters. The monks knew well how to place their house and Malbane made a fine choice when lie built the Cisterian Abbey here. Half surrounded by water and half by wooded. slopes it would make a picture of peace and quiet glory. But owing to the extravagance' of the Abbots the monastery got into difficulties. Then King Henry VIII. in his capacity of Defender of the Faith began to take a marked interest in it. Abbot Massy, its chief, was wiser than some of his fellows and took the virtuous course of making the Kings present of everything. This in itself was a great deal better than getting *aged and having the property taken by force, but Abbot Massy in addition was able to retire upon a handsome pension of £5O a year.

div.head: ANOTHER CHESHIRE HERO.
div.p: ANOTHER CHESHIRE HERO.

It is difficult to realize * that these placid villages of Cheshire have reared so many men of war; yet one could make quite a long 'list of Cheshire warriors,many of whom stand out even in the rough days of the peat as fierce fighters. Here lived Lord Combermere, who was as conceited as he was brave, ard who rode the field in a gorgeous uniform that was said to have cost £5OO, quite careless of the fact that his showy dress made a fine mark for the enemy. The French knew him well, and from his gold lace called him "Leon' ' d'or."

A deputation from the East India Company once waited upon the Duke of Wellington. They had tried to cipture Bhurtpore, but it had resisted every attack, and they wanted a strong general. "You can't do better than have Lord Combermere " said the Duke. "He's the man to take Bhurtpore." They hesitated and finally urged that Lord Combermere was "not of any great genius." "I don't care a damn about his genius" said the Duke. "I tell you he's the man to take Bhurtpore." And take it he did

div.head: FROM LABOUR'S STANDPOINT.
div.p: FROM LABOUR'S STANDPOINT.
A.M.

div.head: By Philip Snowden, I.P.
div.p: By Philip Snowden, I.P.

!SHALL STRIKES BE MADE ILLEGAL The epidemic of strikes from which the whole country is suffering has certain 'peculiar features. which deserve attention. Some of our newspapers are finding evidence which appears to satisfy them that there is a growing spirit of irresponsibility among the workers which is leading them to riot and lawlessness. It is pointed out, also, that some recent strikes, the carters' strike at Manchester, for instarce, have been entered upon without the authority of the trade union officials and continued in spite of the entreaties of.the. leaders to resume work.

I do not think that it is really the fact that there is an increase of lawlessness in the conduct of strikes. The recollection of old events gets dim as the years pass, but an effort will call back to memory the remem- brance of incidents in labour disputes of old, where riot and bloodshed occurred more serious than anything which has happened in recent years. Instead of there being a tendency to greater lawlessness, the facts, when contrasted, point rather in the opposite direction. There was the prolonged lock-out in the shipbuilding trade last year which was not marked by a single outbreak of disorder on the part of the men. For ten months there have been some ten thousand miners on strike in the Rhondda Valley, and except the outburst in the early days of the dispute, which was little more than good-tempered horseplay on the part of a number of young men, there has been the most perfect order, and the people have borne their sufferings in

A few incidents have been reported in connection with the strikes at Hull and Manchester where bodies of men have come in contact with the police. But when one remembers the number of men on strike such incidents only serve to throw into Igreater relief the respect for law which is shown by the great body of strikers. It should be remembered that a strike lain itself an act of war; it is a decision to let force and not reason settle a dispute. Under any circumstances a strike contains all the materials for a conflagration. Men's passions can be easily roused at such times. They are burning under a sense of wrong, and that is a state where reason is not always seated firmly on her throne. ANOTHER FEATURE.

We have to take into consideration, too, the character or type of the men who have I been concerned in the recent strikes. Dock I labourers and other casual workmen con- nected with the transport trades, from the very nature of their work and lives, are not easily disciplined, and have a rather' weak regard for the majesty of the law. They are men who never have any reserve of funds and a week of a strike brings them and their wives and children to a state of starvation. The stories one hears of from Hull and Manchester of the sufferings of the families of the strikers are painful beyond the power of words to describe. They give us some idea of how true it is that one-half the world doesn't know how the other half lives. It must be difficult for starving people to I have much respect for law, and therefore, taking everything into consideration, the wonder is not that there are occasional con- flicts between the police and others at such times, but that such occurrences are not more frequent. It should be remembered, too, that when a strike takes place it is an opportunity for all the loafers and undesir- ables to join in the excitement and o profess Ito belong to the ranks of honest labour. The few cases of disorder which have occurred in the recent strikes are due in the main to this class of person. A WRONG CONCLUSION. _ .

It is not correct to come to the conclusion that thtre is an increase of the spirit of rowdyism in labour disputes. Recent strikes have been as free from such features as strikes are ever likely to be. It is as unreasonable to expect war to be carried on with smooth phrases as a labour dispute to be entirely free from occasional outbreaks of temper. There is no comparison between the way in which a strike is conducted in this country and in America. I was in New York last year when the carriers strike was on, and no insurance company would have risked a dollar on the life of any man who attempted to run the blockade.

But another feature of recent strikes is perhaps something more novel. Alf these strikes have been in trades where there was , little or no trade unionism. The men who I have come out on strike for the imognition of the urion are men who in four cases out of five never paid a cent to a trade union, and I who never will if they can help it. The dockers were supposed to come out at Hull,l , Liverpool, and Manchester to help the sea- men to get their demands, the foremost of which were the recognition of the Union and the abolition of the Federation Ticket. But that wasn't the reason at all. The dockers 'saw that the seamen were getting wages

advances, and they were determined to share in whatever might be going. When they got their advances there was an end of their sympathy with the seamen, who are left without the recognition of their union. . .

The men who have been striking to get the dockers' union recognised will, in four 'cases out of five, leave the union within the next few weeks. It always happens at the time of a strike Oat men rush into the Unions by thousands, but when they have got their increases they refuse to pay. These are not the sort of men who are any good to either trade unionism or the labour move- ment. They are the men who would just as soon "blackleg," if it would pay them better to do it. lrade unionism is not going to be helped by men who profess a sympathy with it only when they are going to gain some immediate advantage by doing so. The kind of man trade unionism needs is he who recognises the need for combination with his fellows at all times, and who is as ready to make sacrifices for principle as he is to receive benefits. A REGRETTABLE FEATURE. . _

----- A third feature of recent strikes is the way in which the men have acted in opposition to the advice of their leaiers. It is in some senses unfortunate that this rebellion has been successful in certain cases. A small advance in wages may be paid for too dearly if it is at the coat of impairing the discipline of the organisation. The government of a trade union should be in the hands of the members, who should decide upon its policy with the advice of those qualified to guide them. But the decisions should be arrived at in a proper way, and it should be regarded as a treacherous act for minorities to take matters into their own hands. The very first principle of trade unionism is majority Lrule. That is what they are fighting for in regard to the Osborne decision. . THE REAL MORAL. —. . _

IF The fourth feature of the recent strikes is the way in which it has been brought home to us that a labour dispute is something more than the business of the two parties directly concerned. The interference with the trans- port trade has resulted in thousands of pounds worth of goods being ruinod, and pric:.s sent up to famine point. The advo- cates of the general strike may have got some idea of what that would mean. It would not be the rich who would suffer. They would be able to buy, the workers would be at starvation within a week. The public have an interest in these disputes. They have a right to protest against incon- venience and loss because some employers and workmen are at loggerheads. The public have a right to knock these two heads together to shake some sense up, if there be any. The present system of industry will only be tolerated so long as it does not annoy the public too much. Too many strikes such as the recent ones will compel the public to take steps to settle them by compulsion.

div.head: IRISH AFFAIRS. NOTES FOR IRISH READERS.

UNION OF YOUNG LIBERALS.

The two democracies of Great Britain and Ireland have seldom had a fiollr onion than that witeereed at Alexandra lark, Manehester, in Saturday, when, as previously ansounced in this column, the young Liberaleof Manchester, NeHord and oliatriet, organised • monster demonstration in suppoit of the present Government. Although Mr. %Chant Jones, Junior Whip, was prevented by illness from attending, the huge crowd that githered in the Perk realised that they had not come in vain when Mr. Joseph Devlin, M.P. commenced to address them. This little man, Catholic end Nationalist, sent by the democrats of Belfast to represent then in the Imperial Parliament, has a wonderful cratorical power, and at each platform of thie immense gathering be met with response, of remarkable enthusiasm. I am lying on what I firmly believe to be my deathbed. Oh, you needn't contradict me. A man generally hap • pre- monition when the end has really come. I only mention the fact to let you know that on such occasions we don't tell lies, se a rule We're a bit afraid of the old traditiona of childhood- the Great White Throne, and the opened Books, and the Judgment, and the anger of the God who made us, and the un- I dying sorrows of the Redeemer who gave Hio life for us. I mention these things, not be- cause I am in any sense • religious man,. but because it never vie my habit to tell lies, I and still less so to tell them now."

"You are excited very much by this talk. log, sir," said Mary. "You ought to lie quiet and go to sleep." "Sleep, child?" said old Henshall. "I shall not sleep all night. I never was no wide awake in my life. And why should I sleep, Mary Gray? Sleep is clone at hand—days, weeks, months, years of sleep. Why should not I stay awake while I can? I shall sleep myeelf into dust all too soon—all too—soon. But, Mary, my dear, I like you for some things, but not altogether. I have always ncticed a want in you. You're not as 'Metier, as you might he." "I— sir?" said Mary. "I repeat it, Mary; you're not as straight as you might be. You do little things that are not strictly honourable. I have watched you, and I know; little things that—for in. stance—Becky could never do. "Mr. Benetton," said Mary, Moved, she did not know why, "how can you possibly compare Rebecca Henshall and me? How wide apart are our liven and our destinies! I am very poor. I bare to struggle hard. If you were to turn Inc out, air, I should not know where to go for my daily bread." Towards morning the nick man fell into an uneasy doze. He lay on his back, breathing somewhat stertorously, his hands lying prone outside the bedclothes, his face highly coloured from the fever which was consum- ing him. It was then that Mary Gray, very, very softly, rose from her seat and, going to- wards the bed, slightly pulled down the bed- clothes with fingers so steady that they did not hhako in the very least. She touched the soft woollen collar which surrounded the sick man a neck, and found what she ex- pected to find, a narrow black ribbon be- neath it. The moment she touched the rib- bon old Henshall moved and groaned, mur- muring to himself : •• I have it safe, Gerard Lonsdale ; valu- able—yes: ifs price beyond rubies; but I save it safe.

Then he turned abruptly on his aide away from Mary, who had sunk, trembling now exceedingly, on a chair by the bedmide. She had made a discovery. She had found out where Robert Henshall kept the diamond. It must, indeed, be of untold value when he wore it round his neck all night long, Mary had been thinking. Two thousand pounds wan worth a great deal. It wan—to use a well-known proverb—a bird in the hand, a plump, fat, substantial aort of bird; and the possession of the diamond and her possible marriage with Arnold were—to follow the same metaphor—cloaely resembling the two birds in the bush. One was safe and certain and comfortable, the other was vague, dangerous, uncertain, and probably, when

all was said and done, the reverse of com- fortable. Of your,, the two bird. in the bush might mean untold wealth; while two thousand pounds, Mary knew well, would at the beet oely mean a shelter from the storm, starvation, or little better, cleared away from her path. Nevertheless, all night long she thought a great deal of the two thousand pounds and the promise she must make were she to secure that sum of money. She knew Robert Hegelian too well to doubt for u moment that he would not present hes with the money, without hedging her in with conditons, which would make it impossible for her to marry /mold lleepe. Sir,—We of the National SeflUl'e League Cannot mildly turn "the other cheek," alien a question of National honour and existence ra at stake. Accord- ingly, akin we read datiseroue fallacies, such as times, contained in Mr. C. E. Parker's emlaught on our policy, printed in the "Examiner of July nth, however decently they may he draped in the language of thenaht, and however much we may respect the : writer personally, we most ray plainly why we con- eider them ill-digaded and unsound. This simple effusion reads as if Mr l'arker hail Lost skimmed : through Carlyle's attack on the unfair voluntary system, and misunderstood Catlyle's meaning, and bad Sr St swallowed wholesale the words of some ' worthy mini,ter alto spoke of every war as wicked and every soldier sea butcher, and had then, without any reflection, sat down to fill a cclumn of his party

Mr. Parker. in Ids firat paragraph, writes of rational strvice if it was se.vi•ude for a free people to adopt national training. They have, and are, vmiog fur it, and all the signs of the times show that we Anglo-Saxons will soon How their democratic example. One of the most encouraging signs is the fact that respectable gentle- ' men, who all tht ir lives carry mobrellas, who shudder at the ides of carrying a title, even they write reams on this subject !
